sections.h2: What should a seller know about Lebanon, PA?
sections.html:
Lebanon is a compact city of about 26,500 people where most homes are older, many are rentals, and the typical owner's home is valued at $156,500. That price level means repairs, taxes and closing costs take a large share of any sale, so the details below are worth reading before you set a price.

The city is also Lebanon County's seat of government, 26 miles east of Harrisburg and 88 miles northwest of Philadelphia. It covers just 4.17 square miles, which works out to about 6,435 people per square mile. The mid-2025 estimate is 26,479, down 1.1 percent from the April 2020 base after growing 5.2 percent between 2010 and 2020.

Sellers can choose an agent, a sale by owner or a cash offer for the house in its present state. Whichever you pick, the deed is recorded at the courthouse on South 8th Street and the county treasurer holds the tax records.

sections.h2: How did Lebanon become the city it is?
sections.html:
George Steitz founded the town in 1740 under the name Steitztown. European settlers had arrived around 1720, the town was laid out in 1753, it incorporated as a borough in 1821 and became a city on November 25, 1885. Population passed 14,000 by 1890 and peaked at 30,045 in 1960 before sliding to 24,461 in 2000.

Manufacturing built much of the housing. The Union Canal ran along the north side from 1828 to 1885, San Giorgio pasta has been made here since 1914, and a large Bethlehem Steel mill once operated in the city. Lebanon bologna, first made here before the 1780s, still carries the city's name. The Quittapahilla Creek drains the city westward toward the Susquehanna.

  • Neighboring municipalities: North Lebanon, South Lebanon, West Lebanon and North Cornwall townships.
  • Schools: the Lebanon School District, which serves the city and West Lebanon Township, plus a Harrisburg Area Community College campus and the Lebanon County Career and Technology Center.
  • Weather: about 46 inches of precipitation and 24 inches of snow in a typical year, with January averaging about 30 degrees and July about 74. Gutters, roofs and basements on older homes get tested every winter.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Lebanon homes?
sections.html:
Lebanon has more renters than owners, lower incomes than the state's suburbs and a younger, more diverse population. Fewer than half of homes are owner occupied, so landlords are a large share of both sellers and buyers.

With rent near $992 against a $156,500 home value, the rental market is a major buyer of Lebanon houses. A seller of a tenant-occupied property should expect investors to ask for the rent roll, the license and the last inspection results.

sections.h2: What are the City of Lebanon's rental license rules?
sections.html:
Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the city must be licensed, and each parcel with rental units needs its own application. The rules matter to a seller because a buyer inherits the license history.

  • A $25 penalty is added every 60 days a fee stays unpaid after billing.
  • Renewal is delayed or denied if money is owed to the city or code violations are open.
  • The owner must keep a contract with a licensed trash hauler on file, and a property manager must be within 20 miles of the city limit.
  • Grass and weeds cannot exceed 12 inches, snow and ice must come off sidewalks within 24 hours after a snowfall ends, and inoperable or unlicensed vehicles cannot sit on a premises more than 5 days.
  • Smoke alarms and carbon monoxide detectors are required, and a license revoked for unsafe conditions costs $100 to reinstate.

Questions go to the city's code enforcement office at 717-639-2800, option 2, at 735 Cumberland Street. If the house is a rental, ask for a copy of the current license and any notice of violation before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: What permits and zoning rules can slow a Lebanon sale?
sections.html:
The city's Building and Zoning Division, part of Public Works, runs permits and zoning. A zoning permit is required for building or altering a structure, adding an addition, demolishing or moving one, and putting up fences, decks, sheds and garages. It is also required for a change of use, a swimming pool or hot tub deeper than 18 inches, and a sign.

Construction inspections are done by outside code inspection firms under contract, and the city asks for at least 24 hours' notice. If a prior owner built a deck or shed without a permit, a buyer's inspector may find it. Settle that question before listing, or ask the zoning office what the city would require.

The city zoning ordinance defines 10 districts. A Zoning Hearing Board hears variance and special exception requests.

sections.h2: How do county taxes and the Tax Claim Bureau affect a Lebanon sale?
sections.html:
The Lebanon County Treasurer collects the county real estate tax, the city tax and, now, the Lebanon City School District bill, so one office can tell you whether anything is owed on a city parcel. A tax certification costs $15 per parcel from the Tax Claim Bureau, and requests by mail need a stamped, self-addressed envelope.

Delinquent taxes pass to the Tax Claim Bureau each January. The owner receives a certified mail notice of the amount owed and a payment deadline of the last working day of June the following year. About 17 months after that first notice the bureau mails a notice of sale. Buyers at the upset sale take the property subject to judgments, liens and mortgages, and bidders must pre-register for a $25 fee. The 2026 upset sale list set the sale date for October 12, 2026, and that date has passed.

A seller behind on taxes should pay or arrange the balance before closing. Once a property is on the sale list, the process follows a fixed bureau and court calendar.

sections.h2: How are assessments appealed and the deed recorded in Lebanon County?
sections.html:
County annual assessment appeals must be filed with the Board of Assessment Revision before the 4:30 closing time on September 1 each year, and the county's rules treat a late notice as filed for the next year. The filing fee for a residential property of one to four units is $50 and is not refunded. You or an authorized representative must attend the hearing, and the board can raise, lower or keep the assessment.

Filings go to the Assessment Office at 400 South 8th Street, Room 118. The county also lets owners view their records free on DataScout, using the control number and web password printed on the tax bill.

The Recorder of Deeds is in Room 107 of the same courthouse, open on weekdays, and accepts cash or check only. Most documents come back the following business day, and the Assessment Office must certify the parcel identifier before a deed records. Realty transfer tax is 1 percent at the state level, and the recorder's office collects it with any local share.

sections.h2: When does a cash offer work well for a Lebanon house?
sections.html:
A cash sale fits best for a house that needs repairs, a rental with open code items, a vacant property or an estate. It is also useful when tax delinquency puts the house on a calendar you cannot move.

Price comparison matters here because the median value is modest. Add up the commission, repairs, transfer tax and months of ownership on a listing, and compare that net with a cash figure. To ask for an offer on a Lebanon house in its present state, contact Cash Home Buyers.

faqs.q: Does Lebanon require a rental license?
faqs.a: Yes. Every dwelling unit or rooming unit offered for rent in the City of Lebanon must be licensed, with a separate application for each parcel that has rental units.

faqs.q: When are Lebanon County assessment appeals due?
faqs.a: September 1 each year, filed with the Board of Assessment Revision at the Assessment Office on South 8th Street. A residential appeal costs $50.

faqs.q: How long do I have to pay delinquent taxes before a Lebanon County tax sale?
faqs.a: Taxes go to the Tax Claim Bureau each January, and the payment deadline is the last working day of June the following year. A notice of sale follows about 17 months after the first notice.

faqs.q: Where do I record a deed in Lebanon?
faqs.a: At the Lebanon County Recorder of Deeds, Room 107 of the courthouse at 400 South 8th Street. The office takes cash or check and can also accept electronic recording.

faqs.q: Which school district serves the City of Lebanon?
faqs.a: The Lebanon School District, which covers the city and West Lebanon Township. The county treasurer now collects its tax bill for city parcels.
